sentences.text: This dinosaur is recognized by tall ridges running along the side plates of its neck armor and a prominent ridge on the front of its thigh bone.
Remains were unearthed at the Salitral Moreno site located near General Roca within the Río Negro Province of Argentina.
Early fragments found in 1996 were often called the Argentine ankylosaur before formal naming.
In 2022, a research team led by Facundo Riguetti and Victoria Arbour officially named the new species Patagopelta cristata based on fresh skeletal material.
The genus name combines the local term Patago with the Greek word pelta, which translates to shield.
The species name cristata translates to crested, highlighting the large ridges on its neck shields and leg bones.
A single thigh bone found measures just 25 centimeters in length.
It likely used a unique frond-like structure at the end of its tail for defense, a trait shared with related genera.
Recent findings indicate this animal was more robust, heavily armored, and larger than its relatives Stegouros and Antarctopelta.
Currently, the Paleobiology Database records only one known occurrence of this species.
Taxonomically, it falls within the bird-hipped dinosaur group known as Ornithischia.
It is placed inside the family Nodosauridae.
Analysis by Riguetti and colleagues in 2022 assigned it to the subfamily Nodosaurinae, differing from earlier studies that suggested Panoplosaurini.
This extinct ankylosaurian roamed Argentina during the Late Cretaceous, spanning from the upper Campanian to the lower Maastrichtian ages.
Its existence is dated to the Maastrichtian stage, occurring between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Contemporary ecosystems included birds such as Lamarqueavis and Limenavis, pterosaurs like Aerotitan, and various marine reptiles.
While originally thought to be a nodosaurid, later evidence points toward Parankylosauria, with 2024 studies linking it to Antarctopelta and 2026 reports by Agnolín supporting this placement.
